pills.meaning: To fix a problem, organize something messy, or deal with a situation until it's resolved.
nuances: Natives use it constantly at work and at home — the natural way to say you'll handle something.
vs. solve: 'solve' is for puzzles/equations; 'sort out' is for real-life messes.
vs. fix: 'fix' is for broken things; 'sort out' is for confusing or disorganized situations.
examples: Don't worry about the schedule conflict — I'll sort it out with the manager today.
I finally sorted out my inbox. It was a complete mess.
pills.translation: resolver / organizar / dar um jeito em

similar.note: resolver pensando, encontrar a solução mentalmente

pills.extra: Nativos usam "get it sorted" (UK) como forma curta: "Leave it with me, I'll get it sorted."

practice.question: My internet keeps dropping. I need to ______ it ______ before my meeting tomorrow.
practice.full: I need to sort it out before my meeting tomorrow.

pills.meaning: To think of and produce an idea, plan, solution, or answer — especially when you need one.
nuances: Highlights the creative effort of producing something from your own head.
vs. think of: 'think of' is just having the thought; 'come up with' is delivering the result.
vs. invent: 'invent' is for products/devices; 'come up with' works for ideas, excuses, names, plans.
examples: We need to come up with a better name for this project by Friday.
I don't know how he comes up with these excuses — they get more creative every time.
pills.translation: bolar / ter uma ideia / inventar (solução, plano, desculpa)
pills.extra: Collocations: come up with an idea / a solution / a plan / an excuse / a name.

practice.question: The client rejected our proposal, so we have to ______ ______ ______ something new by Monday.
practice.full: We have to come up with something new by Monday.

pills.meaning: Extremely busy — with so much work or so many tasks that you can barely handle them.
nuances: The natural answer to 'How's your week?' when you're overloaded. Informal but professional-safe.
vs. busy: 'busy' is neutral; 'swamped' is busy times ten.
vs. overwhelmed: 'overwhelmed' adds emotional stress; 'swamped' is just volume of work.
examples: Can we reschedule? I'm completely swamped this week.
She's been swamped with emails since she got back from vacation.
pills.translation: atolado / soterrado de trabalho / na correria total
pills.extra: Collocation-chave: swamped WITH — swamped with work / emails / requests.

practice.question: Sorry I didn't reply yesterday — I was ______ ______ patient reports all day.
practice.full: I was swamped with patient reports all day.
